```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Every estimate tidycreel returns carries a `unit`. This page explains where
that unit comes from, why it is sometimes `NA`, and what happens when a rate
and an effort are in different units.

The rule is short: **a unit is derived, never declared.** tidycreel states a
unit only where it did the arithmetic that produces it. Everywhere else the
unit is `NA`, meaning unknown.

```
count side:     count x period length (add_counts, period_length_col)  -> angler-hours
                anything else                                           -> NA
interview side: trip hours x party size (add_interviews, n_anglers)    -> angler-hours
                trip hours alone                                        -> party-hours
rate:           fish / (interview-side unit)
total:          rate x effort -> fish, only when the two units cancel; otherwise NA
```

```{r load, message = FALSE}
library(tidycreel)
```

## Why there is no default unit

A count column arrives as a column of numbers. It may hold instantaneous head
counts (how many anglers were present at one moment) or effort the caller has
already expanded to the day. The two look identical. `example_counts`, used in
several examples, is the second kind: its `effort_hours` column is daily
effort, not a head count.

If tidycreel assumed one of them, it would print a confident unit on a number
that may be in the other. A wrong label is worse than none, because nothing
downstream would question it. So the package asserts a unit only where it
can see why the unit is true.

## The count side

An instantaneous count becomes effort when it is multiplied by the length of
the period it was randomised within, $T_d$ (the fishing day, or the shift). A
count of 12 anglers on a 14-hour day is $12 \times 14 = 168$ angler-hours.
`add_counts()` does that multiplication when it is given `period_length_col`,
and only then does the design record its effort as angler-hours.

`example_season_counts` holds one instantaneous count per sampled day and the
day's length:

```{r season-counts}
head(example_season_counts, 3)
```

```{r count-with-td}
design <- creel_design(example_season_calendar, date = date, strata = day_type)
with_td <- add_counts(design, example_season_counts,
  period_length_col = daylight_hours
)
estimate_effort(with_td)
```

The effort is in angler-hours because the package multiplied each count by its
`daylight_hours`.

Leave the period length out, and the same counts are summed as they stand:

```{r count-without-td}
without_td <- add_counts(design, example_season_counts,
  count_col = total_anglers
)
effort_no_td <- estimate_effort(without_td)
effort_no_td
effort_no_td$unit
```

The printout has no `Unit:` line, because the unit is `NA`, and the estimate
is 219 rather than 3,066. Every day in
these data is 14 hours long, so the two differ by exactly that factor. The
warning says what happened: the counts were expanded without a period length.
The package does not know whether `total_anglers` was a head count (in which
case the answer is missing its $T_d$) or effort already expanded (in which
case 219 is right in some unit it cannot see). It reports the number and
leaves the unit unknown.

Two other routes:

- **Daily effort from `prep_counts_daily_effort()`.** That helper hands
  `add_counts()` effort the caller has already worked out for each day. There
  is no instantaneous count left to expand, so the period-length warning does
  not fire, but the unit is still `NA`: the caller chose the input column, and
  the package did not see the multiplication that made it.
- **Aerial designs.** `creel_design()` requires `h_open` for an aerial survey,
  and `estimate_effort()` multiplies the count by it, so aerial effort from
  `estimate_effort()` is angler-hours. `estimate_effort_aerial_glmm()` still
  reports an unknown unit; that is a known defect, open as issue #492.

## The interview side

A rate's denominator is the effort in the interviews. An interview records how
long a party fished. That is party-hours. To make it angler-hours,
`add_interviews()` multiplies trip hours by party size, which it does when it is
given `n_anglers`.

```{r interviews-with-party-size}
with_party <- add_interviews(with_td, example_season_interviews,
  catch = catch_total, effort = hours_fished, harvest = catch_kept,
  trip_status = trip_status, n_anglers = n_anglers
)
estimate_catch_rate(with_party)
```

Without `n_anglers`, the same interviews give a rate per party-hour, and
`add_interviews()` warns that it has no party size:

```{r interviews-without-party-size}
without_party <- add_interviews(with_td, example_season_interviews,
  catch = catch_total, effort = hours_fished, harvest = catch_kept,
  trip_status = trip_status
)
estimate_catch_rate(without_party)
```

The two rates are not interchangeable. The party-hour rate is the angler-hour
rate times the effort-weighted mean party size of the complete trips, 1.69 in
these data.

Bus-route and ice estimators build effort from the interviews themselves
(a sum of each trip's effort over its inclusion probability), so their effort
unit also comes from this side: party-hours without `n_anglers`. Pope et al.
(Chapter 17, unpublished draft) define the bus-route effort estimate the same way, as
"estimated total party-hours of effort".

## How units combine

A total is a rate times an effort. Its unit is the product of their units:

$$\frac{\text{fish}}{\text{angler-hour}} \times \text{angler-hours} = \text{fish}$$

That cancels only when the rate's denominator is the effort's unit. tidycreel
composes the unit from its two inputs rather than writing `"fish"` on every
total, so any other combination comes out `NA`:

| Effort unit  | Rate unit         | Total unit |
|--------------|-------------------|------------|
| angler-hours | fish/angler-hour  | fish       |
| party-hours  | fish/party-hour   | fish       |
| angler-hours | fish/party-hour   | `NA`       |
| `NA`         | fish/angler-hour  | `NA`       |
| `NA`         | fish/party-hour   | `NA`       |

The first two are catches. The second is the bus-route or ice case without
`n_anglers`: effort and rate both come from the interviews, both in
party-hours, and the party-hours cancel. Here is the first:

```{r total-cancels}
estimate_total_catch(with_party)
```

With the rate per party-hour, the product warns and has no unit:

```{r total-mismatch}
total_party <- estimate_total_catch(without_party)
total_party
total_party$unit
```

The total is 1,134 instead of 674. Multiplying a rate per party-hour by
angler-hours inflates the catch by about the mean party size, which is the
error the `NA` and the warning exist to stop. The 1.68 ratio is close to the
rate ratio of 1.69 but not equal to it, because the total is built stratum by
stratum.

The same derivation runs wherever a unit is built from another:

- **Trips** are effort divided by mean trip length, so they inherit the
  effort's actor: angler-hours give angler-trips, party-hours give
  party-trips, and an unknown effort unit gives an unknown trip unit.
- **Effort per acre** (`estimate_effort_per_acre()`) appends "/acre" to
  whatever the effort's unit is, so an unknown unit stays unknown.

## What to do with an `NA` unit

An `NA` unit is not an error. The number is still the estimate of *something*;
the package cannot say what. To get a unit:

- give `add_counts()` the period each count was randomised within, with
  `period_length_col`;
- give `add_interviews()` the party size, with `n_anglers`.

If your count column already holds angler-hours, the number is right and only
the label is missing. The package has no way to be told that, on purpose: a
typed unit would be exactly as trustworthy as an axis label, a second place to
write the wrong thing.

## References

- Pope, K. L., et al. Creel surveys. Chapter 17 (unpublished draft).
